subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Edexcel Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Functionalists argue that a key role of education is to...
options: Transmit shared norms and values and create social solidarity
questions.explain: Functionalists such as Durkheim see education transmitting shared culture and creating social solidarity.

questions.q: Émile Durkheim argued that education helps society by...
options: Creating social solidarity and teaching specialist skills
questions.explain: Durkheim argued education creates social solidarity and provides the specialist skills a modern economy needs.

questions.q: Parsons described school as a 'bridge' between the family and wider society because it teaches...
questions.explain: Parsons saw school teaching universalistic, meritocratic values, bridging family and society.

questions.q: Bowles and Gintis's 'correspondence principle' argues that school...
options: Mirrors the workplace and prepares pupils to accept exploitation
questions.explain: Bowles and Gintis argued school corresponds to work, reproducing an obedient, exploitable workforce.

questions.q: The 'hidden curriculum' refers to...
options: The informal lessons, values and attitudes pupils learn (e.g. obedience, hierarchy)
questions.explain: The hidden curriculum is the informal learning of norms and values, such as punctuality and obedience.

questions.q: Paul Willis's study 'Learning to Labour' focused on...
options: A group of working-class 'lads' who formed an anti-school subculture
questions.explain: Willis studied 12 working-class boys ('the lads') whose anti-school subculture led them into low-skilled jobs.

questions.q: Willis argued that the 'lads' ended up in working-class jobs because they...
options: Rejected school and 'saw through' the myth of meritocracy, yet reproduced their class position
questions.explain: Willis showed the lads resisted school but their anti-school culture led them back into working-class jobs.

questions.q: 'Material deprivation' as an explanation for underachievement refers to...
options: Lack of physical/economic resources (e.g. money, space, equipment)
questions.explain: Material deprivation is a lack of money and physical resources that can harm educational achievement.

questions.q: A child with no quiet space or computer to do homework is disadvantaged mainly by...
questions.explain: Lacking physical resources like space and equipment is material deprivation.

questions.q: Bourdieu's concept of 'cultural capital' suggests middle-class children succeed partly because...
options: They possess knowledge, language and tastes valued by schools
questions.explain: Cultural capital is the middle-class knowledge, language and skills that schools reward.

questions.q: In recent decades, national exam results in England show that...
options: Girls generally outperform boys at GCSE
Boys consistently outperform girls at GCSE
questions.explain: Girls have generally outperformed boys at GCSE in recent decades, a key spec trend.

questions.q: The idea that some boys develop 'laddish' anti-school subcultures to appear masculine helps explain...
options: Why some boys underachieve at school
questions.explain: Laddish subcultures value being seen as tough rather than academic, which can lower boys' achievement.

questions.q: Which of these is a school-based explanation for ethnic differences in achievement?
questions.explain: In-school factors like teacher labelling and an ethnocentric curriculum are internal explanations.

questions.q: 'Setting and streaming' refers to...
options: Grouping pupils by ability into different classes or groups
questions.explain: Setting/streaming groups pupils by ability, which can affect labelling and achievement.

questions.q: A 'self-fulfilling prophecy' in education occurs when...
options: A teacher's label leads a pupil to behave in line with that label
questions.explain: A label (e.g. 'bright' or 'troublemaker') can shape a pupil's behaviour so the prediction comes true.

questions.q: Rosenthal and Jacobson's study showed that pupils labelled as 'spurters' by teachers...
options: Improved more, because teachers treated them differently
questions.explain: Their study demonstrated the self-fulfilling prophecy: labelled pupils improved due to teacher expectations.

questions.q: Stephen Ball's research on 'parentocracy' and marketisation argued that...
options: Middle-class parents are better able to use the education market to their advantage
All parents have equal choice of schools
questions.explain: Ball argued marketisation gives middle-class ('skilled/privileged') parents advantages in choosing schools.

questions.q: Ball's study of 'Beachside Comprehensive' highlighted how ______ affected pupils' progress.
questions.explain: Ball found banding and labelling shaped pupils' attitudes and achievement at Beachside.

questions.q: 'Vocational education' (e.g. apprenticeships, BTECs) is designed mainly to...
options: Provide work-related skills and prepare people for employment
questions.explain: Vocational education provides practical, work-related skills to prepare people for specific jobs.

questions.q: Sociologists describe the gap in results between richer and poorer pupils as the...
options: Achievement gap linked to social class
questions.explain: Differential achievement by social class is often called the class achievement gap.
